ai_summary: Scotland’s electrical grid is currently demonstrating exceptional renewable performance, driven by wind generation reaching a robust 4.4 GW. This surge in clean power has suppressed regional carbon intensity to a remarkably low 32 gCO2/kWh, underscoring Scotland's pivotal role in the broader British decarbonization trajectory. However, this high-yield generation period highlights persistent structural friction across the transmission network, with total wasted energy accumulating to 221.1 MWh. This curtailment is a direct consequence of north-to-south export bottlenecks, where transfer capacity across key network boundaries—most notably the B6 border—is insufficient to evacuate surplus power toward southern demand centers. While an ultra-low carbon footprint reflects superior generation capability, discarding clean megawatt-hours imposes elevated balancing costs through constraint payments funded by consumers. To maximize asset productivity and mitigate these economic inefficiencies, grid planners must accelerate critical transmission reinforcements, such as subsea HVDC links, while fast-tracking localized co-located battery storage. In the immediate term, expanding flexible industrial demand tariffs and regional green hydrogen production will be essential to absorb this stranded volume, transforming forced curtailment into valuable grid resilience and dispatchable domestic energy.
